name: Mississippi
summary_text: Mississippi stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred self-selection of gender on passports and visas; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued only as M or F on supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records. Screening at US checkpoints adds an outing risk through secondary screening, devices and pat-downs, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European countries, adjusted their travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States during 2025.  Facilities access inside Mississippi is restricted by state law. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright facility-use bans; Mississippi enacted such bans across 2024 and 2025 and defines sex by birth in statute. Some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances, and a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in April 2025, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's law.  The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its 'Worst Laws Passed' category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people, on a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric. A July 2026 national risk assessment separately flagged four states as 'Do Not Travel' for trans people and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights. Mississippi's own 2024 session shows the legislative direction: the SAFER Act, which would have restricted trans people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories, and the 'Women's Bill of Rights,' which would have codified a binary definition of sex determined at birth and curtailed legal recognition of trans identities, both died on 29 April 2024 after lawmakers failed to agree compromise versions.  Court treatment of gender-transition recognition is documented. On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented; Justice James D. Maxwell II's majority opinion referred to the trans boy as a 'minor female' and cited the 2023 REAP Act, which bans surgical and non-surgical treatments for transgender minors, as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving gender-transition assistance. The 2023 statute is the state-level care restriction; nationally, gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and federal measures including Executive Order 14187, Department of Justice subpoenas to over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19, the removal of specialised LGBTQ youth services from the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and proposed Medicaid reimbursement bars for transgender patients under 18 constrain care, several of them blocked or enjoined in court.  Violence risk is measurable and federal prosecution has followed. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale. A July 2026 state-by-state analysis of killings of trans women, adjusted for undercounting across 2008-2025, records 6.6 such killings per 100,000 trans women annually in Mississippi, above the 6.0 per 100,000 US general-population homicide rate printed alongside it, and finds that legal tier does not sort violence, with both worst-law and safest-law states carrying high rates. Federal custody adds further documented harm: from 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025, and in December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists characterised as promoting "radical gender ideology."

sources.title: Religious Liberty Accommodations Act - HB 1523 (2016)
sources.documents: Protects individuals, religious organizations, some businesses acting on beliefs that marriage is one man-one woman, sexual relations confined to such marriage, gender determined at birth; enables refusal of services
sources.detail: Scheduled effective July 1, 2016; enjoined June 30 by U.S. District Judge Carlton W. Reeves; injunction lifted June 23, 2017 by Fifth Circuit for lack of standing; guided by Alliance Defending Freedom

name: Missouri
summary_text: A visitor to Missouri stands under the national framework of the United States in every setting. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F, so a trans visitor's documents may not match their presentation. Airport screening and visa decisions follow the same national rules, including the State Department's February 2025 announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25', with a declaration of a gender other than sex assigned at birth capable of being treated as fraud and a permanent bar.  Missouri prohibits gender-affirming medical care for minors. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 after a St Louis judge denied a preliminary injunction against it on 29 August 2023. The statute bars hormones and puberty blockers for under-18s unless the patient was already in treatment, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors.  The SAFE Act also bars MO HealthNet Medicaid coverage of the prohibited care, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes violating providers to licence revocation. CNN reports that the law additionally bars Missouri Medicaid from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, and that doctors who breach the ban can lose their state medical licence and be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment.  Litigation over the ban has failed at every stage so far. Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner filed suit on 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court on behalf of three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA, seeking to block Senate Bill 49 before its 28 August 2023 effective date. A Missouri judge upheld the law on 25 November 2024, and on 13 January 2026 the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously upheld the ban on gender-transition surgeries, cross-sex hormones and other gender-affirming care for minors, quoting the 2025 United States Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's similar ban. Counsel for the plaintiffs said they would appeal. The ban has been in force since 28 August 2023 and remains in force.  The statute carries a 2027 sunset enacted as a Republican-Democrat concession, but lawmakers have moved to make it permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative also seeks to ban such care indefinitely. The plaintiffs continue toward trial on the merits.  Correctional custody carries its own care exclusion. Governor Mike Kehoe signed an appropriations law, effective 2 July 2026, barring state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri thereby became the seventh state, and the second in 2026 after Oklahoma, to ban gender-affirming care for inmates; Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while similar Idaho and Georgia measures were blocked by federal courts.  A trans visitor to Missouri is unlikely to encounter the SAFE Act unless accompanying a minor who needs medical care, but anyone detained in a Missouri jail, prison or correctional centre loses access to state-funded hormone therapy and transition surgery under both the SAFE Act and the 2026 appropriations law.
